title: Shrink-Back Rule
description: The shrink-back rule (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2)) narrows a failed business component to the next most significant subset that meets the four-part test.
summary: The shrink-back rule, codified at Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(b)(2), lets U.S. taxpayers claiming the federal R&D tax credit under IRC § 41 narrow a failed business component to its next most significant subset of elements until a subset meets the Four-Part Test, including the 80 percent substantially-all requirement. It preserves eligible research expenses rather than excluding them.

body.text: The shrink-back rule, codified at Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(b)(2), lets U.S. taxpayers claiming the federal R&D tax credit under IRC § 41 narrow a failed business component to its next most significant subset of elements until a subset meets the Four-Part Test, including the 80 percent substantially-all requirement. It preserves eligible research expenses rather than excluding them.
Executive Summary: Mandate, Regulatory Mechanism, and Core Corrections

The Shrink-Back Rule—formally titled the "Shrinking-back rule" in Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(b)(2) (26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2))—is a foundational regulatory mechanism governing the federal Credit for Increasing Research Activities (commonly known as the Research and Development or R&D Tax Credit) under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) § 41 (26 U.S.C. § 41). When a taxpayer develops or improves a multi-faceted product, process, computer software system, technique, formula, or invention, the statutory qualification criteria—known as the Four-Part Test under IRC § 41(d)(1)—must first be applied separately at the level of the overall discrete "business component" pursuant to IRC § 41(d)(2)(A)–(B). A central requirement of the Four-Part Test is the "Substantially All" threshold codified in IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6), which mandates that 80 percent or more of a taxpayer's research activities with respect to a business component—measured on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis—must constitute elements of a process of experimentation conducted for a qualified purpose, defined under IRC § 41(d)(3)(A) as a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality.

When an initial business component encompasses substantial routine engineering, commercial system integration, or aesthetic design work, the ratio of experimental activities to total developmental activities is diluted and frequently falls below the 80 percent threshold, causing the macro business component to fail the Four-Part Test. Rather than forfeiting the tax credit across the entire engineering initiative, Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) directs the taxpayer to iteratively "shrink back" the boundary of the qualification assessment to the "most significant subset of elements" (or "next most significant subset of elements," per the regulatory illustration in Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(3)) of the business component. This downward iterative evaluation continues through progressively narrower technical tiers until either a subset of elements of the business component is reached that satisfies all requirements of IRC § 41(d)(1), or the most basic element of the product is reached and fails to satisfy the test. As clarified in the preamble to the final regulations under Treasury Decision (T.D.) 9104 (69 FR 22, effective January 2, 2004, applicable to taxable years ending on or after December 31, 2003), the Shrink-Back Rule functions as an inclusionary, enabling provision rather than an exclusionary penalty, ensuring that legitimate Qualified Research Expenditures (QREs, defined under IRC § 41(b)) embedded within broader commercial developments remain eligible for the federal research credit.
1. Regulatory Codification of the Shrink-Back Rule (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) vs. § 1.41-4(d))

Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4, the Shrinking-back rule is codified exclusively at Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2), and its canonical motorcycle engine and carburetor illustration is codified at Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(3). By contrast, Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(d) governs Recordkeeping for the research credit, requiring taxpayers to retain records in sufficiently usable form and detail to substantiate credit eligibility in accordance with IRC § 6001 and Treas. Reg. § 1.6001-1. Confusing the substantive boundary-narrowing rule (§ 1.41-4(b)(2)) with the evidentiary substantiation mandate (§ 1.41-4(d)) undermines legal precision in IRS examination responses and protest briefs.
2. Statutory Citation for Non-Qualified Cosmetic and Style Factors (IRC § 41(d)(3)(B) vs. § 41(d)(4))

Under the Internal Revenue Code, research relating to style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors is barred from satisfying a qualified purpose under IRC § 41(d)(3)(B) ("Certain purposes not qualified") and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)(ii), whereas IRC § 41(d)(4) separately enumerates eight discrete categories of excluded activities, such as research after commercial production, customer adaptation, and duplication of an existing business component.
3. Statutory Citation for the Business Component Definition (IRC § 41(d)(2) vs. § 41(d)(1))

While IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(ii) requires that qualified research be intended to be useful in the development of a new or improved business component of the taxpayer, the statutory mandate to apply the qualification tests separately to each business component and the explicit statutory definition of "business component" are codified in IRC § 41(d)(2)(A)–(B).
4. Treatment of Manufacturing Processes vs. Products (IRC § 41(d)(2)(C))

Under IRC § 41(d)(2)(C) ("Special rule for production processes") and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(1), any plant process, machinery, or technique for the commercial production of a business component is statutorily treated as a separate business component—and never as part of, or a shrink-back subset of, the product being manufactured. Product development and manufacturing process development must therefore be evaluated and shrunk back along strictly independent tracks.
6. IRS Form 6765 Section G Effective Date and Reporting Rules

Per the updated Instructions for Form 6765 (Rev. December 2025), Section G (Business Component Information)—which mandates component-by-component reporting for business components comprising at least 80 percent of total QREs or up to the Top 50 business components—is optional for tax years beginning before 2026 (unless the taxpayer is filing an amended return for a research credit refund or credit) and becomes mandatory for tax years beginning after 2025. While preparing a contemporaneous Shrink-Back Rationale Memorandum is an essential internal audit-defense practice under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(d)—and detailed component-level factual disclosures are mandatory at the time of filing for amended-return refund claims under IRS Chief Counsel Memorandum 20214101F and Form 6765 Column 49(f)—the Form 6765 Instructions do not require attaching a narrative memorandum to a timely filed original return.
I. The Statutory Context: IRC Section 41 and the Business Component Framework
A. The Foundation of Qualified Research Expenses (QREs) vs. Activity Qualification

A taxpayer's eligibility to claim the federal R&D Tax Credit under IRC § 41 is predicated upon incurring expenditures that qualify as Qualified Research Expenses (QREs) under IRC § 41(b) while carrying on a trade or business. Under IRC § 41(b)(1)–(3), QREs consist strictly of the sum of in-house research expenses and contract research expenses. In-house research expenses encompass three exhaustive statutory categories. First, they include employee wages—as defined in IRC § 3401(a), excluding any wages taken into account in computing the work opportunity credit under IRC § 51(a)—paid or incurred for "qualified services," which consist of engaging in qualified research, directly supervising qualified research, or directly supporting qualified research under IRC § 41(b)(2)(B). Second, in-house research expenses include amounts paid or incurred for supplies used in the conduct of qualified research, defined in IRC § 41(b)(2)(C) as any tangible property other than land, improvements to land, and property of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation. Third, they include amounts paid or incurred to another person for the right to use computers in the conduct of qualified research under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(iii) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2. Contract research expenses under IRC § 41(b)(3)(A) equal 65 percent of any amount paid or incurred by the taxpayer to any person other than an employee of the taxpayer for qualified research, a statutory inclusion rate that increases to 75 percent for payments to qualified research consortia under IRC § 41(b)(3)(C) and to 100 percent for eligible energy research payments made to eligible small businesses, universities, or federal laboratories under IRC § 41(b)(3)(D).

IRC § 41 establishes a rigorous structural bifurcation between the credit computation phase (governed by IRC § 41(a) and § 41(c)) and the activity qualification phase (governed by IRC § 41(d)). In the computation phase, the credit operates as an incremental tax incentive reported on IRS Form 6765 (Credit for Increasing Research Activities) under either the Regular Credit method or the Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC) method. Under the Regular Credit method (IRC § 41(a)(1) and § 41(c)(1)–(3), reported in Form 6765 Section A), the research credit equals 20 percent of the excess of current-year QREs over a base amount calculated by multiplying the taxpayer's fixed-base percentage—derived either from historical QRE-to-gross-receipts ratios for taxable years beginning after December 31, 1983, and before January 1, 1989, under IRC § 41(c)(3)(A), or under the start-up company rules of IRC § 41(c)(3)(B), subject in all cases to a statutory ceiling of 16 percent under IRC § 41(c)(3)(C)—by the average annual gross receipts of the taxpayer for the 4 preceding taxable years under IRC § 41(c)(1)(B), with a statutory minimum base amount equal to 50 percent of current-year QREs under IRC § 41(c)(2). Under the Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC) method (IRC § 41(c)(4), reported in Form 6765 Section B), the credit equals 14 percent of so much of the current-year QREs as exceeds 50 percent of the average QREs for the 3 preceding taxable years under IRC § 41(c)(4)(A), or 6 percent of current-year QREs if the taxpayer had no QREs in any of the 3 preceding taxable years under IRC § 41(c)(4)(B).

Before any expenditure can enter the IRC § 41(b) QRE pool or influence the IRC § 41(c) incremental base computation, the underlying technical activity must satisfy the substantive definition of "qualified research" under IRC § 41(d). The Shrink-Back Rule in Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) operates exclusively within this IRC § 41(d) activity-qualification phase, serving as the boundary-defining mechanism that determines which specific engineering subsystems may feed costs into the IRC § 41(b) expenditure ledger.
B. The Gateway: The Four-Part Test and Initial Business Component Assessment

Under IRC § 41(d)(1), Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(2), and Chapter 5 of the IRS Audit Techniques Guide (ATG) (Credit for Increasing Research Activities IRC § 41 — Qualified Research Activities, June 2005), an activity constitutes qualified research only if it is not barred under IRC § 41(d)(3)(B) or § 41(d)(4) and satisfies all four cumulative requirements of the statutory Four-Part Test.

First, under the Section 174 / Section 174A Expense Eligibility Test (IRC § 41(d)(1)(A)), the research expenditures must be eligible to be treated as expenses under IRC § 174—or, following the enactment of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) on July 4, 2025, as domestic research or experimental expenditures under newly enacted IRC § 174A. Pursuant to Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1), expenditures represent research and development costs in the experimental or laboratory sense if they are incurred in connection with the taxpayer's trade or business and are intended to discover information that would eliminate uncertainty concerning the capability or method for developing or improving a product or the appropriate design of that product. Because the OBBBA restored immediate expensing options for domestic R&E under IRC § 174A while retaining capitalization requirements for foreign R&E under IRC § 174, tax departments must ensure that general ledger accounts mapped to IRC § 174A also capture component-level uncertainty data required by IRC § 41(d)(1)(A).

Second, under the Discovering Technological Information Test (IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(i) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(3)–(4)), the research must be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is technological in nature, meaning the process of experimentation fundamentally relies on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science. As finalized in T.D. 9104 (codified at Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(3)(ii)), a taxpayer need not seek information that exceeds, expands, or refines the common knowledge of skilled professionals in the field, nor is the research required to succeed in achieving its technical objectives. Furthermore, under the regulatory patent safe harbor of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(3)(iii), the issuance of a patent under 35 U.S.C. § 151—other than a design patent issued under 35 U.S.C. § 171—constitutes conclusive evidence that the taxpayer has discovered information that is technological in nature and intended to eliminate uncertainty.

Third, under the Business Component Test (IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(ii) and § 41(d)(2)), the taxpayer must intend the application of the discovered technological information to be useful in the development of a new or improved business component of the taxpayer. Under IRC § 41(d)(2)(B), the term "business component" is statutorily defined as any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention which is to be (i) held for sale, lease, or license, or (ii) used by the taxpayer in a trade or business of the taxpayer.

Fourth, under the Process of Experimentation Test (IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)–(6)), substantially all of the research activities must constitute elements of a process of experimentation—defined in Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i) as an evaluative process designed to evaluate one or more alternatives (such as modeling, simulation, or a systematic trial-and-error methodology) to achieve a result where the capability or method of achieving that result, or the appropriate design of that result, is uncertain as of the beginning of the taxpayer's research activities—conducted for a qualified purpose. Under IRC § 41(d)(3)(A) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)(ii), a qualified purpose relates exclusively to a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality of the business component.

Crucially, IRC § 41(d)(2)(A) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) mandate that the Four-Part Test be applied first at the level of the discrete business component as a whole. When a taxpayer defines an initial business component broadly—such as an entire commercial vehicle, an integrated industrial manufacturing system, a consumer smart watch, or an enterprise-wide software implementation—that macro component inevitably combines core experimental engineering with routine mechanical design, standard commercial component integration, ordinary quality control testing, or aesthetic styling.

Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6), the "Substantially All" requirement is satisfied only if 80 percent or more of a taxpayer's research activities with respect to the business component, measured on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis (and explicitly determined without regard to Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(d)(2), which governs the separate 80 percent employee wage inclusion rule), constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose under IRC § 41(d)(3). Practitioners must distinguish here between IRC § 41(d)(3)(B) and IRC § 41(d)(4): the statutory bar on research relating to style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors is codified in IRC § 41(d)(3)(B) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)(ii), whereas IRC § 41(d)(4) enumerates excluded activities such as post-commercial-production research, customer adaptation, and duplication. Whenever non-experimental activities or non-qualified cosmetic design work exceed 20 percent of the total research activities for the initial business component, the macro component fails the 80 percent threshold under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6), triggering the technical necessity and regulatory mandate to apply the Shrink-Back Rule under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2).
II. The Shrink-Back Rule: Mechanics, Purpose, and Regulatory Linkage
A. Direct Relationship to the 80% Substantially All Requirement

The Shrink-Back Rule in Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2)—originating in the legislative history of the Tax Reform Act of 1986 and refined through T.D. 8930 in 2001, REG-112991-01 in December 2001, and T.D. 9104 in January 2004—operates in direct mathematical tandem with the 80 percent "Substantially All" requirement of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6). Appreciating their precise operational interplay requires analyzing both macro-level passage and macro-level failure.

When a business component achieves macro-level passage—meaning 80 percent or more of the research activities with respect to the discrete business component constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose—the "Substantially All" requirement is satisfied at that initial level without any need to shrink back. Under the 80 percent / 20 percent inclusion rule of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6), the remaining 20 percent or less of the taxpayer's research activities with respect to that business component also qualify within the credit-eligible activity base—even though they do not themselves constitute elements of a process of experimentation—so long as those remaining research activities satisfy the requirements of IRC § 41(d)(1)(A) (the Section 174 / Section 174A experimental expense eligibility test) and are not otherwise excluded under IRC § 41(d)(4). For example, in Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(8), Example 4, an automobile manufacturer updates a vehicle model to lower the hood for improved aerodynamics while maintaining adequate airflow to the engine and cooling system; because evaluative activities (designing, modeling, simulating, testing, and retesting alternative configurations for the hood, air intake, and cooling system) represent 85 percent of the overall update activities and non-evaluative activities represent 15 percent, the 85 percent ratio meets the ≥ 80% threshold, and 100 percent of the update activities qualify as eligible research activities.

Tax practitioners must also account for a documented administrative discrepancy regarding this 20 percent residual bucket. As highlighted in the April 2025 Tax Notes Federal analysis by Grant Thornton, the June 2005 IRS Audit Techniques Guide states that the remaining ≤ 20% balance of non-experimentation activities "may qualify," whereas the authoritative text of the final regulations in Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6) states definitively that the test "is satisfied" so long as the remaining ≤ 20% meets IRC § 41(d)(1)(A) and is not barred by IRC § 41(d)(4). Because final Treasury Regulations promulgated via notice-and-comment rulemaking carry superior legal authority over internal IRS examination guides, the mandatory inclusion rule of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6) governs.

Conversely, macro-level failure occurs whenever non-evaluative engineering, routine assembly, or non-qualifying design exceeds 20 percent of the total research activities for the overall business component. As Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i) emphasizes, mere uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a business component (such as uncertainty regarding its appropriate design) does not establish that all activities undertaken to achieve that new or improved business component constitute a process of experimentation. When non-evaluative activities dilute the process-of-experimentation ratio below 80 percent at the macro level, Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) prevents a punitive "all-or-nothing" disallowance by narrowing the business component boundary to a smaller developmental subset where the concentration of systematic experimentation meets or exceeds 80 percent.
B. The Mandatory Iterative Process and the Next Most Significant Subset of Elements

Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) and Chapter 5, Section b of the IRS Audit Techniques Guide, the Shrink-Back Rule is not an elective cherry-picking mechanism permitting taxpayers to jump directly from a failed macro product to isolated micro-tasks. Rather, it mandates a sequential, top-down, three-step iterative methodology.

In Step 1 (Overall Discrete Business Component Assessment), the requirements of IRC § 41(d) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a) must be applied first at the level of the discrete business component—that is, the overall product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention to be held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in a trade or business of the taxpayer. Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) explicitly establishes failure at this initial tier as a condition precedent: "This shrinking-back rule is applied only if a taxpayer does not satisfy the requirements of section 41(d)(1) and paragraph (a)(2) of this section with respect to the overall business component".

In Step 2 (Stepping Down to the Next Most Significant Subset of Elements), if the requirements of IRC § 41(d)(1) are not met at that first macro level, then those qualification requirements are applied at "the most significant subset of elements" (phrased in the regulatory illustration of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(3) as "the next most significant subset of elements") of the product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention to be held for sale, lease, or license.

In Step 3 (Continuous Downward Iteration Until Qualification or Exhaustion), if the first shrunk-back subset also fails to meet the 80 percent "Substantially All" threshold or any other prong of the Four-Part Test, the boundary is narrowed again to the next subordinate technical tier. Under the express mandate of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2): "This shrinking-back rule is to continue until either a subset of elements of the product that satisfies the requirements is reached, or the most basic element of the product is reached and such element fails to satisfy the test".

A critical statutory correction is required regarding the treatment of manufacturing processes within this hierarchy. That sequence conflicts with IRC § 41(d)(2)(C) ("Special rule for production processes") and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(1), which mandate that any plant process, machinery, or technique for the commercial production of a business component is treated as a separate business component—and not as part of the business component being produced. Consequently, research activities relating to the development of a product are not qualified research unless the requirements of IRC § 41(d) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4 are satisfied for the product without taking into account research activities relating to the development of its manufacturing process, and vice versa. When shrinking back a physical product, the downward iteration moves strictly through structural subsets of the product itself (Overall Product → Major Subsystem / Sub-Assembly → Specific Component → Most Basic Element); if a commercial manufacturing process also fails at the macro process level, that process must be shrunk back along its own independent track of process sub-stages or machinery subsystems.

Substantiating what constitutes the "next most significant subset of elements" represents a primary locus of IRS examination friction. When a complex project comprising four major subsystems (Subsystems A, B, C, and D) fails the 80 percent test at the macro level because Subsystems B, C, and D involve routine commercial engineering, the taxpayer must present engineering architecture records and cost-accounting ledgers demonstrating that Subsystem A represents a discrete, technically significant subset where technological uncertainty was resolved through a process of experimentation (≥ 80%). Because the regulations do not define "significance" via an arbitrary dollar threshold, taxpayers must anchor the hierarchy in functional engineering decomposition (such as bill-of-materials tiers or software system architecture) coupled with segregated sub-ledger cost codes.
C. The Conceptual Role: An Enabling Inclusionary Provision, Not an Exclusion Mechanism

A recurring misconception during R&D tax examinations is the assertion by examining agents that the Shrink-Back Rule operates as an exclusionary device designed to disqualify research expenditures. Both the express text of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) and the regulatory preamble to T.D. 9104 (69 FR 22, January 2, 2004) refute this interpretation. The final sentence of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) states unambiguously: "The shrinking-back rule is not itself applied as a reason to exclude research activities from credit eligibility". Similarly, in the preamble to T.D. 9104, the Department of the Treasury and the IRS addressed public commentators' concerns that the 2001 proposed regulations (REG-112991-01) implied that not all qualified research expenses would be eligible for the credit as a result of the rule, explaining that the regulatory text was specifically revised "to clarify that the rule is not intended to exclude qualified research expenses from the credit, but rather is intended to ensure that expenses attributable to qualified research activities are eligible for the research credit for purposes of section 41(d)(1)".

Activities that are statutorily barred from credit eligibility are non-qualified from the outset by operation of IRC § 41(d)(3)(B) and IRC § 41(d)(4), not by operation of the Shrink-Back Rule. Specifically, IRC § 41(d)(3)(B) bars research conducted for non-qualified purposes relating to style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors. In parallel, IRC § 41(d)(4)(A)–(H) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(1)–(10) categorically exclude eight statutory classes of activities from qualifying as research. These eight excluded categories encompass research conducted after the beginning of commercial production of the business component under IRC § 41(d)(4)(A); research related to the adaptation of an existing business component to a particular customer's requirement or need under IRC § 41(d)(4)(B); and research related to the reproduction or duplication of an existing business component, in whole or in part, from a physical examination of the business component itself or from plans, blueprints, detailed specifications, or publicly available information under IRC § 41(d)(4)(C). The statutory exclusions under IRC § 41(d)(4) further bar surveys, routine data collection, efficiency surveys, activity relating to management functions or techniques, market research, testing, or development (including advertising or promotions), and routine testing or inspection for quality control under IRC § 41(d)(4)(D). Additionally, IRC § 41(d)(4)(E) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(6) exclude research with respect to computer software developed by, or for the benefit of, the taxpayer primarily for internal use by the taxpayer (Internal Use Software or IUS), unless the software is developed for use in an activity that constitutes qualified research, is developed for use in a production process meeting the requirements of IRC § 41(d)(1), or satisfies the regulatory three-part High Threshold of Innovation test. Finally, the statute excludes research conducted outside the United States, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, or any possession of the United States under IRC § 41(d)(4)(F); research in the social sciences, arts, or humanities under IRC § 41(d)(4)(G); and any research to the extent funded by any grant, contract, or otherwise by another person or governmental entity under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H).

As noted in the preamble to T.D. 9104, when a broader commercial development project contains these statutorily excluded activities alongside genuine technological experimentation, applying the Shrink-Back Rule allows the taxpayer to redefine the business component boundary downward so that excluded or routine activities are left outside the component denominator, isolating and preserving the eligible experimental subcomponent.
D. Comparison of R&D Qualification Mechanisms and the Shrink-Back Rule

body.text: III. Practical Application, Regulatory Illustrations, and Worked Hypothetical Examples
A. The Canonical Motorcycle Engine and Carburetor Illustration (Treas. Reg. Section 1.41-4(b)(3))
The authoritative regulatory illustration of the Shrink-Back Rule is set forth verbatim in Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(3) (26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(3)):

"Example. X, a motorcycle engine builder, develops a new carburetor for use in a motorcycle engine. X also modifies an existing engine design for use with the new carburetor. Under the shrinking-back rule, the requirements of section 41(d)(1) and paragraph (a) of this section are applied first to the engine. If the modifications to the engine when viewed as a whole, including the development of the new carburetor, do not satisfy the requirements of section 41(d)(1) and paragraph (a) of this section, those requirements are applied to the next most significant subset of elements of the business component. Assuming that the next most significant subset of elements of the engine is the carburetor, the research activities in developing the new carburetor may constitute qualified research within the meaning of section 41(d)(1) and paragraph (a) of this section."

Tracing the operational sequence of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(3) demonstrates how the regulatory mechanism functions across four sequential phases. First, in the Level 1 Application (Overall Engine) phase, Company X must apply the requirements of IRC § 41(d)(1) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a) to the entire modified motorcycle engine as a single discrete business component. Second, in the Level 1 Failure phase, when viewed as a whole, the modifications to the existing engine design include substantial routine mechanical adjustments, standard mounting adaptations, and conventional integration testing that do not involve resolving technological uncertainty through a process of experimentation. Because these routine engine modifications dilute the experimental ratio below the 80 percent "Substantially All" threshold of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6), the overall engine project fails to qualify at Level 1.

Third, in the Level 2 Shrink-Back Iteration (The Novel Carburetor Subset) phase, pursuant to Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) and (b)(3), Company X steps down to the "next most significant subset of elements" of the engine—namely, the development of the new carburetor.
B. Application in High-Technology, Medical Devices, Industrial Systems, and Software Development

In modern hardware manufacturing, medical technology, heavy industrial engineering, and enterprise software architecture, breakthrough R&D is routinely embedded inside large-scale commercial deployments dominated by standard engineering, regulatory packaging, or configuration work. Examining industry applications demonstrates how Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) preserves credit eligibility across diverse technical sectors while exposing the accounting pitfalls that lead to judicial disallowance.

At the macro product level (Level 1), the project includes external housing and casing, aesthetic watch straps (statutorily barred from satisfying a qualified purpose under IRC § 41(d)(3)(B)), commercial power-management integration, and routine functional software interfaces totaling $850,000 (85 percent of total project costs), alongside $150,000 (15 percent of total project costs) dedicated to developing a novel sensor mechanism / optical bio-sensor undergoing systematic trial-and-error experimentation to resolve performance and reliability uncertainty. Evaluated as a complete watch or medical device at Level 1, only 15 percent of the project involves a process of experimentation (15% < 80%), causing Level 1 to fail the "Substantially All" requirement. By applying Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) to shrink back to the sensor mechanism / optical bio-sensor subcomponent (Level 2), the taxpayer excludes the $850,000 of non-qualifying housing, strap, and routine interface costs from the business component boundary and validly claims the $150,000 in QREs directly tied to the experimental sensor.

In heavy industrial engineering (documented in KBKG's technical analysis, Mastering the Business Component Test for R&D Tax Credit Success), a manufacturer develops a $2,000,000 industrial system where the overall macro system fails the Four-Part Test due to standard structural fabrication and conventional assembly, but $600,000 of the development expenditures relate to a qualifying subcomponent involving novel heat-exchange technology. Shrinking back under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) enables the manufacturer to evaluate and claim the $600,000 heat-exchange subcomponent independently. Conversely, as demonstrated in Trinity Industries, Inc. v. United States, 691 F. Supp. 2d 688 (N.D. Tex. 2010), aff'd in part and vacated in part, 757 F.3d 400 (5th Cir. 2014), where a shipbuilder claimed entire first-in-class marine vessels as qualified business components and failed the 80 percent "Substantially All" test at the whole-vessel level, the federal courts recognized that the Shrink-Back Rule legally permits testing smaller subcomponents or subsystems, provided the taxpayer maintained books and records capable of identifying and quantifying the expenses connected to those smaller subcomponents. Because Trinity Industries used a high-level project accounting system that pooled costs at the whole-vessel level without segregating subsystem expenditures, neither the district court nor the Fifth Circuit could apply the Shrink-Back Rule to salvage the credit.

Because the vast majority of a commercial ERP deployment consists of routine vendor configuration, data migration, and standard workflow adaptation—activities that fail the Four-Part Test and trigger internal-use software exclusions under IRC § 41(d)(4)(E) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(6)—the $5,000,000 "ERP Project" fails at Level 1. However, during the deployment, the company's software engineers architected a custom Middleware API Module to bridge two incompatible legacy databases, conducting systematic experimentation to resolve acute technical uncertainty regarding real-time data integrity and transaction latency. By shrinking back the business component definition from the $5,000,000 macro ERP implementation to the discrete Middleware API Module, the taxpayer isolates and claims $200,000 in qualified software development wages.

body.text: C. Worked Hypothetical Example: Multi-Level Cost Segregation, Employee Wage Nexus (Treas. Reg. Section 1.41-2(d)(2)), and R&D Credit Computation

To demonstrate the exact mathematical interaction between the Shrink-Back Rule (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2)), the 80 percent "Substantially All" activity test (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6)), the separate 80 percent employee wage inclusion rule (IRC § 41(b)(2)(B) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(d)(2)), and the statutory contract research limitation (IRC § 41(b)(3)(A)), consider the following comprehensive worked calculation for MedTech Corp in Tax Year 2026.
1. Hypothetical Project Facts and Level 1 (Macro Component) Assessment

MedTech Corp incurs $2,000,000 in total domestic development costs during Tax Year 2026 to build a new commercial Automated Patient Monitoring System, which constitutes the Overall Product at Level 1. The macro product architecture consists of two major functional subsystems tracked under separate sub-ledger work breakdown structure codes. The first major subsystem, Subsystem A (Optical Micro-Fluidic Sensor Array), incurs total research and development costs of $500,000, of which $460,000 relates directly to systematic trial-and-error experimentation (evaluating alternative laser wavelengths and micro-channel geometries to eliminate technical uncertainty regarding blood-analyte detection accuracy) and $40,000 relates to non-evaluative IRC § 174A technical baseline documentation for the sensor array. The second major subsystem, Subsystem B (Commercial Display Console, Casing, and Power Supply), incurs total development costs of $1,500,000, of which only $140,000 involves experimental thermal dissipation testing and $1,360,000 consists of routine mechanical casing design, cosmetic industrial styling barred under IRC § 41(d)(3)(B), and standard off-the-shelf component integration.
When MedTech Corp applies the "Substantially All" test of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6) on a cost basis at Level 1 (Overall Automated Patient Monitoring System), the ratio is computed as follows:

Because 30.0% < 80.0%, the overall Automated Patient Monitoring System fails the Four-Part Test at Level 1. Without applying the Shrink-Back Rule, MedTech Corp's eligible QREs for the entire $2,000,000 development effort would be $0.
2. Level 2 Shrink-Back Assessment (Treas. Reg. Section 1.41-4(b)(2))

Pursuant to Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2), MedTech Corp shrinks back the business component definition to the next most significant subset of elements: Subsystem A (Optical Micro-Fluidic Sensor Array), excluding Subsystem B entirely from the component boundary. Recomputing the "Substantially All" ratio under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6) for Subsystem A alone yields:
Level 2 Substantially All Ratio (Subsystem A) = $460,000 / $500,000 = 92.0% ≥ 80.0%

Because 92.0% ≥ 80.0%, Subsystem A satisfies the "Substantially All" requirement under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6). Furthermore, under the 80 percent / 20 percent inclusion rule of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6), because at least 80 percent of Subsystem A's research activities constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose, the remaining 8.0% ($40,000) of non-evaluative research activities for Subsystem A also qualify within the eligible activity base—as they satisfy IRC § 41(d)(1)(A) / IRC § 174A and are not excluded under IRC § 41(d)(4)—bringing the eligible activity pool for Subsystem A to 100 percent ($500,000 of gross activity costs).
3. Granular QRE Quantification for Shrunk-Back Subsystem A (IRC Section 41(b))

Having qualified Subsystem A as a valid business component under IRC § 41(d), MedTech Corp traces its specific expenditure categories under IRC § 41(b) to Subsystem A using contemporaneous time logs, supply ledgers, and third-party contractor invoices.

For Researcher 1 (Lead Sensor Physicist — Dedicated ≥ 80% Employee under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(d)(2)), annual Form W-2 wages equal $200,000. Contemporaneous time logs verify that Researcher 1 spent 85 percent of total annual working hours (1,700 of 2,000 hours) performing qualified services directly on Subsystem A, and 15 percent (300 hours) on general administrative meetings. Under the employee wage "substantially all" rule of IRC § 41(b)(2)(B) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(d)(2)—which is applied on an employee-by-employee basis and is legally distinct from the business-component "Substantially All" activity test of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6)—because 85% ≥ 80%, 100 percent of Researcher 1's annual wages ($200,000) qualify as wage QREs.

For Researcher 2 (Electro-Mechanical Engineer — Split-Time < 80% Employee), annual Form W-2 wages equal $160,000. Because 50% < 80%, the 80 percent wage safe harbor of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(d)(2) does not apply, and only the exact time-tracked proportion linked directly to qualifying Subsystem A ($160,000 × 0.50 = $80,000) may be included as wage QREs.

For Qualified Supplies (IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii) & (C)), non-depreciable micro-fluidic cartridges, chemical reagents, and optical sensor wafers consumed directly in Subsystem A prototype testing total $120,000, which is 100 percent includible ($120,000).

For Contract Research Expenses (IRC § 41(b)(3)(A)), MedTech Corp paid $100,000 in gross fees to an unrelated third-party optical laboratory for laser-calibration testing on Subsystem A pursuant to a written agreement entered into prior to the performance of the research, under which MedTech Corp bears the financial risk of failure and retains substantial rights to the research results in accordance with Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e). Applying the statutory 65 percent inclusion limitation under IRC § 41(b)(3)(A) ($100,000 × 0.65) yields $65,000 in contract research QREs.

body.text: 4. Resulting Federal R&D Tax Credit Calculation (IRC Section 41(c)(4) vs. Section 41(a)(1))

Summing the four validated expenditure categories ($200,000 + $80,000 + $120,000 + $65,000) yields MedTech Corp's Total Validated QREs for Shrunk-Back Subsystem A of $465,000. Assume MedTech Corp incurred average annual QREs of $400,000 over the preceding 3 taxable years (2023–2025) and elects the Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC) method under IRC § 41(c)(4)(A) on IRS Form 6765 Section B:
ASC Base Amount = 50% × $400,000 = $200,000
Incremental Excess QREs = $465,000 − $200,000 = $265,000
Gross ASC Research Credit (14% Rate) = $265,000 × 0.14 = $37,100

If MedTech Corp makes the reduced credit election under IRC § 280C(c)(3) on Form 6765 Item A / Line 26 in order to preserve 100 percent of its domestic research and experimental deduction under IRC § 174A (avoiding the statutory deduction reduction equal to the gross credit under IRC § 280C(c)(1)), the net tax credit equals 79 percent of the gross credit (reflecting the maximum 21 percent corporate tax rate under IRC § 11(b)): $37,100 × 0.79 = $29,309.
IV. Compliance, Substantiation, Judicial Scrutiny, and Computational Distinctions
A. Recordkeeping and Audit Defense Requirements (IRC Section 6001, Treas. Reg. Section 1.41-4(d), Chief Counsel Memo 20214101F, and Form 6765 Section G)
Promulgated under T.D. 9104 (69 FR 22, January 2, 2004), Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(d) provides verbatim:

"(d) Recordkeeping for the research credit. A taxpayer claiming a credit under section 41 must retain records in sufficiently usable form and detail to substantiate that the expenditures claimed are eligible for the credit. For the rules governing record retention, see § 1.6001-1. To facilitate compliance and administration, the IRS and taxpayers may agree to guidelines for the keeping of specific records for purposes of substantiating research credits."

In the regulatory preamble to T.D. 9104, Treasury and the IRS noted that while earlier regulations issued under T.D. 8930 in January 2001 had imposed a separate, specific "contemporaneous documentation" requirement beyond IRC § 6001, the December 2001 proposed regulations (REG-112991-01) and January 2004 final regulations (T.D. 9104) eliminated that separate regulatory mandate so that Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(d) aligns directly with the general permanent books-and-records standard of IRC § 6001 and Treas. Reg. § 1.6001-1. Nevertheless, as federal courts (including United States v. Bayer Corp. and Trinity Industries, Inc. v. United States) and Chapter 5 of the IRS Audit Techniques Guide emphasize, the taxpayer bears the affirmative burden of proof to establish that all requirements of IRC § 41(d)(1) are satisfied separately for each discrete or shrunk-back business component.

To satisfy Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(d) when invoking the Shrink-Back Rule under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2), corporate tax departments must establish a rigorous three-tier structure of proof. First, under Tier 1 (Documenting Level 1 Macro Component Failure), detailed technical and financial records must outline the scope of activities within the initial, discrete business component and demonstrate that non-experimental activities exceeded 20 percent of total research activities, substantiating that the regulatory condition precedent in Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) ("applied only if a taxpayer does not satisfy the requirements of section 41(d)(1) ... with respect to the overall business component") was met. Second, under Tier 2 (Justifying the Level 2 Subset Selection as the "Next Most Significant Subset"), engineering architecture records and a technical rationale memorandum must articulate why the chosen subcomponent or subsystem represents the "next most significant subset of elements" under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2)–(3), linking the narrowed boundary directly to the subsystem where technological uncertainty was resolved through a process of experimentation. Third, under Tier 3 (Proving Direct Cost Nexus for Level 2 QREs Linking IRC § 41(b) to IRC § 41(d)), contemporaneous employee time logs (segregating hours spent on the qualifying shrunk-back component from hours spent on routine integration of the parent product), supply ledgers, and third-party contract invoices must strictly trace expenditures to the shrunk-back subset, confirming that 80 percent or more of the research activities for that specific subset constituted elements of a process of experimentation.

Beyond internal audit-file substantiation, the IRS has embedded component-level reporting directly into Redesigned Form 6765 (Credit for Increasing Research Activities, Instructions Rev. December 2025) and administrative refund procedures. On revised Form 6765, Section E (Other Information) requires taxpayers to report the total number of business components generating QREs during the tax year, officer wages included in QREs, whether any QREs or base amounts were adjusted for IRC § 41(f) acquisitions or dispositions, and whether the ASC 730 Financial Statement R&D Directive was utilized. More importantly, Section G (Business Component Information) is optional for tax years beginning before 2026 (unless the taxpayer is filing an amended return claiming a research credit refund or credit) and becomes mandatory for tax years beginning after 2025, subject to targeted exemptions for qualified small businesses electing the IRC § 41(h) payroll tax offset and taxpayers whose ASC 730 Directive entry on Line 41 represents at least 80 percent of total QREs on Line 48. (This December 2025 IRS Instruction revision supersedes earlier 2024 commentary that had referenced a 2025 effective date prior to the IRS's one-year transition extension.)

Under Section G of Form 6765, taxpayers must itemize each business component accounting for at least 80 percent of total QREs in descending order by QRE size, up to a maximum of the Top 50 business components, aggregating any remaining components under "Aggregate Business Components" in Column 49(c). For each reported business component, the taxpayer must disclose in Column 49(a) the Employer Identification Number (EIN) of the controlled group member conducting the research; in Column 49(b) the Principal Business Activity (PBA) code for the component; in Column 49(c) the business component's unique name or alphanumeric identifier consistent with the taxpayer's books and records used to substantiate QREs; in Column 49(d) the simplified business component type (classified as Product, Process, or All Others); and in Column 49(e), where the business component is computer software, its specific regulatory software classification (Internal Use Software [IUS], Dual Function Software [DFS], Non-IUS commercial software, or Excepted software). Across Columns 50 through 56 of Section G, the taxpayer must report disaggregated wage QREs broken down separately across direct research conduct (Column 50), direct supervision of research (Column 51), and direct support of research (Column 52), alongside total qualified wages (Column 53), qualified supply QREs (Column 54), 65 percent, 75 percent, or 100 percent contract research QREs (Column 55), and total component QREs (Column 56).

Furthermore, when claiming a research credit refund or credit on an amended return (such as Form 1120-X or Form 1040-X), both Form 6765 Column 49(f) and IRS Office of Chief Counsel Memorandum 20214101F (released October 15, 2021, interpreting the specificity requirement of Treas. Reg. § 301.6402-2(b)(1)) require the taxpayer at the time of filing the refund claim to identify all business components to which the IRC § 41 research credit claim relates for that year, and for each business component, to identify all research activities performed, all individuals who performed each research activity, and the information each individual sought to discover. Consequently, whenever a taxpayer relies on the Shrink-Back Rule under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2), the shrunk-back subset itself is the reportable business component in Section G of Form 6765 and must carry a unique alphanumeric identifier tied directly to the general ledger.
B. Judicial Scrutiny of the Substantially All Fraction: Intermountain Electronics, Inc. v. Commissioner and Related Precedents

The IRS actively litigates R&D tax credit claims through the mathematical lens of the 80 percent "Substantially All" rule under IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6). Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6), the "Substantially All" requirement is evaluated for each discrete or shrunk-back business component via the following quantitative ratio:
Substantially All Ratio = (Research Activities Constituting a Process of Experimentation for a Qualified Purpose) / (Total Research Activities With Respect to the Business Component) ≥ 80%

In Intermountain Electronics, Inc. v. Commissioner, Docket No. 11019-19 (T.C. Mar. 14, 2024) (Order), a Utah-based custom electrical equipment manufacturer claimed federal R&D tax credits for tax years 2012 through 2015 for designing and manufacturing custom electrical distribution and control equipment—including switchgears and mobile e-houses—which the taxpayer classified as pilot models under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(4). Intermountain computed its QREs by including the wages of both non-production employees (design engineers) and production employees (fabricators, welders, assemblers, and test technicians), along with production supplies consumed in building the custom units.

The IRS disallowed the credits and moved for partial summary judgment, relying on Little Sandy Coal Co., Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2021-15, aff'd, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023), to argue that production expenses incurred in building a pilot model must be categorically excluded as a matter of law from the numerator of the "Substantially All" fraction while remaining in the denominator. Because Intermountain's non-production design engineering costs represented less than 80 percent of total pilot-model costs, the IRS contended that Intermountain's pilot models mathematically failed the "Substantially All" test.

On March 14, 2024, the U.S. Tax Court denied the IRS's motion for partial summary judgment, holding that Little Sandy Coal "does not foreclose production expenses from being included in the numerator of the substantially all equation". The court ruled that production costs incurred in developing a pilot model can be included in the "Substantially All" numerator if the taxpayer establishes as a factual matter at trial that such production activities constituted elements of a process of experimentation. (In a separate earlier procedural dispute in federal district court involving a refund claim for another year, Intermountain Electronics, Inc. v. United States [D. Utah, July 2021], the district court held that the IRS waived administrative specificity objections by examining the claim on the merits for five years, but dismissed the initial complaint without prejudice with leave to replead because the complaint alleged only conclusory statutory labels—"process of experimentation"—without pleading specific facts describing the experimental process.)

Viewed alongside Little Sandy Coal Co., Inc. v. Commissioner (62 F.4th 287, where the Seventh Circuit held that direct support and supervision activities that are not themselves elements of a process of experimentation cannot be included in the numerator if trial-and-error experimentation is not otherwise proven across 80 percent of the component's activities), Union Carbide Corp. v. Commissioner (T.C. Memo. 2009-50, examining process vs. product experimentation on commercial production runs), Trinity Industries, Inc. v. United States (757 F.3d 400, disallowing whole-vessel claims where subsystem shrink-back lacked segregated accounting records), Suder v. Commissioner (T.C. Memo. 2014-201), and Betz v. Commissioner (T.C. Memo. 2023-84), Intermountain Electronics underscores why the Shrink-Back Rule in Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) is indispensable in pilot-model and custom-manufacturing disputes. If a taxpayer bundles all structural fabrication and assembly labor into an overall pilot model and fails to prove at trial that at least 80 percent of those combined production and engineering costs were integral elements of a scientific process of experimentation, the overall pilot model fails IRC § 41(d)(1)(C). Only if the taxpayer has maintained granular subcomponent cost records under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(d) can it invoke Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) to shrink back from the overall pilot model to the specific electrical, control, or mechanical subsystems that independently satisfy the 80 percent threshold.
C. Proactive Compliance Systems vs. Retrospective Reconstruction

Relying on manual interviews or high-level estimates to apply the Shrink-Back Rule retrospectively—years after expenditures have been incurred and without subcomponent cost codes in the general ledger—carries severe audit disallowance risk because precise cost segregation for the 80 percent calculation degrades rapidly over time. In United States v. Bayer Corp. (Civil Action No. 09-351, Special Master Findings of Fact), the taxpayer's accounting system captured research expenses by general organizational cost center rather than by discrete business component. When challenged in litigation to identify every business component under IRC § 41(d)(2)(A) and prove component-level qualification, Bayer argued that doing so retrospectively would require interviewing vast numbers of researchers and collecting millions of pages of records—a posture that the government successfully attacked as "exactly backwards" under the statutory framework of IRC § 41(d)(2)(A) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(d).

In contrast, proactive compliance architecture integrates the business-component and subcomponent hierarchy directly into project-management, ERP, and time-tracking systems before research costs are paid or incurred. When employee hours (segregated by direct research, direct supervision, and direct support), supply requisitions, and third-party contractor invoices are contemporaneously tagged to specific subcomponents via alphanumeric WBS (Work Breakdown Structure) codes, a shrunk-back claim is immediately verifiable upon IRS examination and seamlessly populates Form 6765 Section G.
D. Differentiation from Computational Consistency and M&A Rules (IRC Section 41(f)(3) and IRC Section 41(c)(5))

Tax professionals must strictly differentiate the Shrink-Back Rule (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) under IRC § 41(d)) from statutory provisions that narrow, adjust, or "shrink" historical base-period figures in the credit computation phase. Under IRC § 41(f)(3)(A) (Acquisitions) and IRC § 41(f)(3)(B) (Dispositions), when a taxpayer acquires or disposes of the major portion of a trade or business—or the major portion of a separate unit of a trade or business—after December 31, 1983, the taxpayer must adjust (increase for an acquisition, or decrease/"shrink" for a disposition) its historical QREs and gross receipts for periods before the transaction so that the base amount and fixed-base percentage accurately reflect the post-transaction business entity. As the IRS Audit Techniques Guide (Chapter 3, Section e(3)) explains, IRC § 41(f)(3) is triggered by acquisitions or dispositions of a viable trade, business, or separate unit, whereas a standalone acquisition or disposition of corporate stock that merely alters controlled-group membership is governed by the controlled-group aggregation rules of IRC § 41(f)(1). Similarly, IRC § 41(c)(5)(A) (Consistent treatment of expenses required) mandates that QREs taken into account in computing the historical fixed-base percentage be determined on a basis consistent with the determination of QREs for the current credit year, regardless of whether the statutory period for filing a claim for credit or refund has expired for those historical base years.

Whereas IRC § 41(f)(3) and IRC § 41(c)(5) are structural, entity-level computational rules that enforce period-over-period financial consistency across historical base periods on Form 6765, the Shrink-Back Rule in Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) is a technical activity-qualification test under IRC § 41(d) focused exclusively on defining component boundaries in the credit year (and, via the consistency rule of IRC § 41(c)(5), requiring parallel component-level qualification standards in base years). Conflating IRC § 41(d) component shrinking with IRC § 41(f)(3) corporate disposition adjustments exposes the taxpayer to examination adjustments on both QRE qualification and incremental credit computation.
V. Grounded Analysis and Strategic Recommendations for Corporate Tax and R&D Teams

The following operational recommendations synthesize statutory, regulatory, and judicial authorities into a defensible compliance framework for corporate tax departments and engineering teams executing Shrink-Back claims under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2).
1. Institutionalize a Centralized Internal Audit Protocol (IAP) Dedicated to Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) Component Decomposition

Corporate tax and R&D departments should establish a formal Internal Audit Protocol (IAP) governing business-component scoping under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) and recordkeeping compliance under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(d). This protocol should require that at project initiation, engineering leads and tax specialists decompose complex R&D initiatives into a documented three-level technical hierarchy—Level 1 Overall Product or Process, Level 2 Major Subsystems or Sub-Assemblies, and Level 3 Discrete Experimental Subcomponents—and assign unique general-ledger sub-project codes to each tier to enable real-time cost segregation. Furthermore, whenever a project involves both product design and commercial manufacturing engineering, the IAP must enforce IRC § 41(d)(2)(C) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(1) by assigning separate business-component identifiers to any plant process, machinery, or production technique so that manufacturing process costs are never commingled with product development costs.
2. Benchmark Internal Definitions of "Significance" and "Process of Experimentation" Against Judicial Precedent

Because Treasury Regulations do not define the "most significant subset of elements" via a fixed dollar threshold under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2)–(3), corporate tax departments should conduct a pre-filing legal review of all shrunk-back components benchmarked directly against Intermountain Electronics, Inc. v. Commissioner (Docket No. 11019-19, T.C. Mar. 14, 2024), Little Sandy Coal Co., Inc. v. Commissioner (62 F.4th 287), Union Carbide Corp. v. Commissioner (T.C. Memo. 2009-50), and Trinity Industries, Inc. v. United States (757 F.3d 400). Where pilot-model production or custom fabrication labor is included within a shrunk-back subsystem, contemporaneous engineering records must substantiate that those production activities were integral to evaluating scientific alternatives under uncertainty pursuant to Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i) and Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(4), ensuring that the numerator of the Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6) fraction remains demonstrably above 80 percent. Tax teams should also evaluate whether measuring the 80 percent "Substantially All" threshold on a cost basis or an "other consistently applied reasonable basis" (such as direct research engineering hours permitted under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6)) provides the most accurate and audit-resilient substantiation across the taxpayer's component portfolio.
3. Mandate Proactive Tax Provisioning and Shrink-Back Rationale Memorandum Integration Aligned with Form 6765 Section G

Tax departments should integrate Shrink-Back sensitivity modeling into quarterly financial forecasting and ASC 740 tax provision calculations, modeling R&D credit capture both at the macro Level 1 component boundary and at the shrunk-back Level 2 / Level 3 subsystem boundaries for high-value capital and engineering projects. For every project where Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) is invoked, the tax department should prepare a contemporaneous Shrink-Back Rationale Memorandum that systematically documents four core evidentiary pillars. First, the memorandum must record the quantitative and qualitative Level 1 macro failure analysis demonstrating why non-experimental activities exceeded 20 percent of the parent business component. Second, it must set forth the engineering architecture justification establishing why the selected Level 2 subset constitutes the "next most significant subset of elements" under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2)–(3). Third, it must detail the specific technological uncertainties and systematic process of experimentation conducted for the shrunk-back subset under IRC § 41(d)(1)(A)–(C) and IRC § 174A. Fourth, it must provide the direct sub-ledger tracing of employee wages (disaggregated across direct conduct, direct supervision, and direct support under IRC § 41(b)(2)(B)), non-depreciable supplies under IRC § 41(b)(2)(C), and 65 percent contract research expenses under IRC § 41(b)(3)(A) to that specific subset.

While this narrative Shrink-Back Rationale Memorandum is retained in the taxpayer's permanent examination file under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(d) rather than attached to a timely filed original return, its structured data fields directly populate the mandatory Section G (Business Component Information) schedule on IRS Form 6765 (Rev. December 2025) for tax years beginning after 2025, as well as the mandatory Column 49(f) and Chief Counsel Memorandum 20214101F factual disclosures required for any amended-return research credit refund claim.

The credit is incremental, calculated via the Regular Credit method (fixed-base percentage × average of preceding 4 years' gross receipts) or the Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC).

Regular credit is 20% over base amount (fixed-base % capped at 16% × 4-year avg gross receipts; minimum base = 50% of current QREs); ASC is 14% over 50% of 3-year avg QREs (or 6% if no QREs in prior 3 years).

Under IRC § 41(d)(1), research must meet the Four-Part Test: (1) § 174 expense eligibility, (2) discovering technological information, (3) business component utility, and (4) process of experimentation for a qualified purpose.
26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1); IRC § 174A added July 4, 2025 (OBBBA), in force 2026
A "qualified purpose" relates to a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality (IRC § 41(d)(3)(A)).
Style, taste, or cosmetic factors are excluded under IRC § 41(d)(4).

Research relating to style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors is barred as a non-qualified purpose under IRC § 41(d)(3)(B) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)(ii), whereas IRC § 41(d)(4) lists eight excluded activity categories.
The Four-Part Test is applied first at the discrete "business component" level.
26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(2)(C); 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(1); Instructions for Form 6765 (Rev. Dec. 2025)

Under IRC § 41(d)(2)(C) (Special rule for production processes), any plant process, machinery, or technique for commercial production is statutorily treated as a separate business component—not as part of, or a shrink-back step from, the product being manufactured.

Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6), the "Substantially All" requirement mandates that 80% or more of research activities for a business component (measured on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis) constitute elements of a process of experimentation.

If the overall business component fails IRC § 41(d)(1), the Shrink-Back Rule applies the test iteratively to the "next most significant subset of elements" until a subset qualifies or the most basic element is reached and fails.
Matches Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) and (b)(3) and IRS ATG Chapter 5.
The regulations explicitly state that the shrinking-back rule is not itself applied as a reason to exclude research activities from credit eligibility; it functions as an enabling/inclusionary rule.
26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2) & Preamble to T.D. 9104 (Jan. 2, 2004), in force 2026

Regulatory illustration: Company X, a motorcycle engine builder, develops a new carburetor and modifies an existing engine design; if the overall engine fails, the test shrinks back to the carburetor.
